title: Maintenance holdback & eviction safety limiter for throughput-preserving upgrades
creator: Aisha Kaur
description:
Summary:
We need a runtime-level 'holdback & safety limiter' that prevents maintenance operations (node drains, preemptive evictions, staged upgrades) from reducing effective dedicated throughput below negotiated guarantees. This feature ensures fleet maintenance can proceed without breaking customer SLAs by calculating and enforcing holdback budgets per maintenance wave and providing an eviction throttle that respects autoscaler and reservation contracts.

Background and motivation:
- Dedicated customers purchase throughput guarantees / reserved capacity. Past maintenance waves incorrectly triggered mass KV cache warmup penalties and token-level latency spikes when several hosts were drained simultaneously.
- Autoscaler and maintenance orchestrator race conditions can cause oversubscription of eviction windows, leading to transient SLO violations.

Goals:
- Prevent simultaneous host drains from exceeding a configured throughput budget for a customer or capacity slice.
- Coordinate with autoscaler to avoid triggering scale-out during maintenance if a cheaper staged holdback is preferred.
- Expose knobs in Dedicated config (holdback_fraction, min_active_hosts, eviction_rate_limit) and telemetry to validate guarantees.

Constraints & non-goals:
- Not responsible for cross-customer global balancing (separate balancer epic).
- Does not change model-level batching heuristics; only controls node lifecycle gating and eviction pacing.

Design overview:
1) Maintenance Wave Planner calculates a conservative throughput impact estimate for a proposed wave by summing per-host historic throughput (30d moving median) + predicted KV cache warmup cost (configurable multiplier).
2) Holdback Budget = max(0, contracted_throughput - predicted_remaining_throughput_except_wave). The planner ensures scheduled evictions only consume up to the holdback budget.
3) Eviction Safety Limiter is a token-bucket style controller per-fleet-slice that caps concurrent evictions and sustains an eviction_rate_limit (hosts/min) and min_active_hosts constraint.
4) Autoscaler integration: a negotiation API where the maintenance planner proposes a wave and the autoscaler can either accept (and scale temporarily) or request reflow with a higher holdback fraction.
5) Graceful failover: if holdback budget would be exceeded, the planner either delays non-critical waves or converts them into transactional micro-drains with KV prewarm hints.

Runtime/config surface:
- New Dedicated config: maintenance.holdback_fraction (string, e.g. "0.15"), maintenance.min_active_hosts, maintenance.eviction_rate_limit, maintenance.predictive_warmup_multiplier.
- Planner API: POST /fleet/{slice}/maintenance/propose -> {wave_id, predicted_impact, allowed_evictions}. Returns approval or counter-proposal.
- Events emitted: maintenance.proposed, maintenance.approved, maintenance.heldback, maintenance.eviction_rate_limited.

Metrics and SLOs to monitor:
- metric: maintenance.holdback_utilization (0-1) per slice
- metric: maintenance.eviction_rate (hosts/min)
- metric: post-maintenance_latency_pctl_95 (tokens/ms) per route/model
- alert: holdback_utilization>0.9 for 10m with post-maintenance_latency_pctl_95 regressing >10%

Testing & rollout plan:
- Unit tests for planner calculations and token-bucket limiter (covered).
- Integration test harness: synthetic traffic replay across a 50-host dedicated slice to validate budget calculations and ensure SLO retention.
- Canary rollout: enable on 1 low-traffic Dedicated cluster (non-SLA) for 2 weeks. Collect holdback_utilization, eviction_rate, and 95p latency.
- Gradual enablement: auto-enable for customers with dedicated contracts after opt-in and a migration window.

Documentation & migration notes:
- Confluence design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Maintenance+Holdback+Design
- Customer-facing doc for Dedicated Console: description of maintenance holdback and the new knobs + migration checklist.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Use historical throughput vs. model-anchored throughput estimate (we chose the conservative history-first approach to avoid under-estimation).
- Whether to allow temporary scale-outs automatically vs. manual approval for large waves. Current plan: autoscaler must approve or provide a counterproposal via API.
